Looking at client.ts now — it's instantiating MongoClient without options, which triggers the mongodb-connection skill since that covers pool configuration for serverless environments. The Vercel serverless pattern with a globally cached client is solid, but settings like `maxPoolSize` and timeouts matter for the setup. I need to invoke that skill before finalizing the review. The keys.ts file uses t3-env which is fine, and it validates the URI with a minimum length check, though I'm considering whether the URL validation should explicitly handle the `mongodb+srv://` scheme.

For collections.ts, the indexes look good — compound indexes all lead with tenantId, and the `sources` unique index on gmail with a partial filter expression is the fix from the commit. The facts collection doesn't need a category index since Atlas Search handles that, and the dossier queries work fine with the existing tenant-anchor index. There's no TTL index, which makes sense since retention is handled elsewhere — sources are purged by Gmail, audio blobs are managed by the caller, and retention windows are config-driven.

The proposals index on tenantId, status, and createdAt descending matches the inbox query pattern. People has a multikey index on emails for the phase-2 email matcher and deduplication. One thing to note: `ensureIndexes` doesn't create the Atlas Search index itself — that's handled separately in the setup script since search indexes use a different API.

Looking at search.ts, the filter uses `equals` on token fields, which is the correct modern pattern. The text search applies fuzzy matching with a max edit distance of 1 for names and typos, though that won't help much with German compound words.

For the superseded exclusion, I'm considering whether to move the `validUntil` and `supersededBy` checks into the Atlas Search query itself using `mustNot` with `exists` operators, rather than filtering post-search with `$match`. That would keep the filtering index-side and avoid the performance cost of post-search matching, though it requires those fields to be indexed in the search mappings. Until"}}]`. This completes the compound filter correctly. The pipeline order is actually fine — `$search` runs first and returns all matching documents, then `$match` filters further, and `$limit` caps the results. It's not the most efficient at scale since `$search` without a limit returns everything, but at the current user volume it's negligible. The `$match` stage after `$search` is allowed in Atlas Search pipelines anyway. I notice the app doesn't surface relevance scoring since there's no `$project` extracting the search score, so results won't be ranked by relevance. The entity-name fuzzy matching in step 2 needs search indexes on the orgs, people, and engagements collections, but the current plan only covers facts. I should flag this as a gap — either add 2-3 more indexes (feasible on M10+ but potentially constrained on Flex tier) or consider a denormalized searchables collection for MVP simplicity. Now looking at the redaction logic in erasure.ts...

The regex filters out identifiers shorter than 3 characters to avoid empty patterns, then joins them with OR logic. The issue is that short names like "Li" or "Bo" slip through unredacted while their emails get caught, and substring collisions are inevitable — "Anna" hiding inside "Susanna", or a surname like "Meyer" matching within "Meyer GmbH" — leading to over-redaction and false positives that create GDPR compliance risk.

The real gap surfaces when matching only the full `person.name` string: if someone is "Stefan Müller" but the transcript mentions just "Stefan", that first name survives erasure entirely. The safer approach would be to split the name into individual tokens of 3+ characters and redact each one with word boundaries to contain false positives, though German umlauts complicate regex word boundaries slightly. — 'r' is word-character, so the boundary after 'r' requires a non-word character next. In "Müllers" (German genitive), the 's' is word-character, so no boundary matches — good, we avoid over-redacting inflected forms. The real gap is under-redaction: we're redacting names from `sources` but leaving them untouched in `facts.text`, which is a bigger concern than the boundary edge cases. This design choice around Article 17 scope is acknowledged as a product decision in the PR. I'm tracing through the regex evaluation order in the object literal—the `.replace()` call resets `lastIndex` to 0 when it finishes, then `.test()` on the email field advances it on a match, but `.replace()` on the subject always starts fresh from 0 regardless of where `lastIndex` was left.

Now checking the distinct/countDocuments logic—the `sourceId` is a scalar value, so that's fine. But I'm noticing the multi-step process isn't atomic; if something fails partway through the erasure, it leaves partial data behind.

For GDPR Article 17 compliance though, the partial states are actually re-runnable and idempotent. If I re-run after a failure, the person still exists but facts are already gone, so the next run just returns zero deletions and re-applies the redaction. The person-not-found early return only triggers when they're already deleted, which is the end state anyway. I could wrap this in a transaction for cleaner semantics, but the sequential idempotent approach is simpler and acceptable. One thing to watch: if the caller gets the report but fails to clean up the audio blob URLs, re-running the erasure will return early since the person is gone, leaving those blobs orphaned.

Actually, that's a real problem — I'm losing track of which sources had their facts deleted because the affected source IDs come from facts that no longer exist. I should flag sources with `audioPendingDeletion: true` in the same pass so a cleanup sweep can find them later, rather than relying on the caller to handle the blob URLs. Since GDPR audio deletion is critical, I'll propose persisting that orphan flag on the source document itself. And I need to verify that voice-type sources store their transcripts in the `content` field.

Now checking the sources schema and person fields — emails are stored as an array of strings and the filter for length > 2 is fine since emails are always longer. The `capturedBy` field references a user (like the CEO), not a KB person, so that's not part of the erasure scope. For the exports in index.ts, the ObjectId re-export isn't done yet but callers can pull it directly from MongoDB for now. The `keys` export follows the standard repo pattern. Query helpers for dossier lookups aren't included by design in this phase.

The core write path invariant — upsert entities, insert facts, resolve proposal — is missing a helper, though the confirmation server action will live in apps/app. A `confirmProposal` helper in the package itself would be a good addition to enforce the "only review queue writes knowledge" constraint as a single testable choke point, maybe for Plan 3. Next I'm reading through the schemas, setup scripts, package config, and tests, then reviewing the MongoDB client before launching the review agents.

I found only minor conflicts in the config and lock files while the core package looks good, though I noted a missing search index and some fire-and-forget blob reporting. Now I'll review the schemas, scripts, plan, and tests.

content.thinking:
Looking at the schema definitions, the validation setup handles runtime checks properly with Zod's ObjectId instance validation. The entity schemas use modern Zod patterns for email validation, keep organization domains as empty arrays by default, and allow person records to exist without an organization ID for standalone contacts. The design is intentionally minimal without notes fields. The facts schema is expanding its category enum to include background and other options.

For the facts lifecycle, there's a constraint where a fact is valid only when both `supersededBy` and `validUntil` are absent — the query logic correctly matches documents where these fields are null or missing, maintaining consistency. The sources schema includes email metadata like forwarded status, Gmail message IDs, and original sender information. There's a recognized gap where the current type enum plus optional objects approach allows invalid states (like a voice source carrying email metadata), and using Zod's discriminated union on the type field would properly model this — flagged as a fast-follow improvement to propose.

For the status lifecycle, sources move through received → transcribed → extracting → proposed → reviewed/failed states, with "reviewed" set once a proposal is resolved. The content field is optional since voice sources lack content before transcription. I'm noticing an erasure consistency issue: redaction masks content, email subject, and original sender, but not forwardedBy (intentionally, since that's a CEO reference), and the redaction query checks those same fields — however, the schema is missing an attachments field entirely, even though the spec calls for "attachments to Blob" in sources documents. This is a schema gap that either needs fixing now or will surface during the email pipeline work, and erasure also doesn't handle orphaned attachment blobs. Worth flagging in review.

For proposals, the entityDraft data is a loose record validated at confirmation time, which is documented. The factDraftAnchorsSchema uses a "some(Boolean)" refinement where empty strings correctly fail the Boolean check since they're falsy.  The proposal status field uses "open" or "resolved" states, and erasure filters consistently on `{status: "open"}`. When erasing an existing person, fact drafts anchored via that person's ID get discarded, but drafts anchored via a new personDraftId (a proposed person) aren't affected — that's correct. Entity drafts for duplicate person proposals remain under-covered, which is an acknowledged open item.

For the setup-indexes script, the IIFE runs without top-level error handling, so unhandled rejections cause Bun to exit non-zero with a stack trace — acceptable for a script, with error narrowing as a noted fast-follow. The search index creation uses the driver v7 signature correctly, though Atlas Search on M0 and Flex tiers has limits (M0 allows only 3 search indexes), and with just the facts_search index currently, there's room before hitting that constraint.

The /people entity would add search indexes, pushing toward the M0 limit of 3 total — worth considering for cost proposals. Package.json looks solid: mongodb ^7.5.0 matches the current driver major, TypeScript 7 is native, and the test script runs cleanly without MONGODB_TEST_URI. I need to review the plan document to verify scope against what's actually implemented, then check the tests and invoke the mongodb-connection skill for client instantiation review before launching the five review agents. The skill result will come through as a separate message with instructions to follow, while the file reads arrive together in one block — that's manageable. I need to watch for when the mongodb-connection skill triggers, specifically when code instantiates or configures a MongoDB client like during a connect() call.

Looking at client.ts now, I see it's creating a new MongoClient with just the URI and no configuration options, so I should invoke the skill.

The schemas look good with Zod v4 and documented invariants, though I noticed the sources are missing an attachments field and the erasure blob-orphan report is ephemeral. Next I'll review the plan doc, test files, and MongoDB connection-config skill to check the MongoClient instantiation.

837	  });

1188	```ts
1189	// packages/knowledge/erasure.ts
1190	import type { Db, ObjectId } from "mongodb";
1191	import { getCollections } from "./collections";
1192	
1193	const REDACTED = "[REDACTED]";
1194	
1195	export interface ErasureReport {
1196	  personDeleted: boolean;
1197	  factsDeleted: number;
1198	  sourcesRedacted: number;
1199	  orphanedAudioBlobUrls: string[];
1200	}
1201	
1202	const escapeRegex = (value: string) =>
1203	  value.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
1204	
1205	export const erasePerson = async (
1206	  db: Db,
1207	  tenantId: string,
1208	  personId: ObjectId
1209	): Promise<ErasureReport> => {
1210	  const { people, facts, sources, proposals } = getCollections(db);
1211	
1212	  const person = await people.findOne({ _id: personId, tenantId });
1213	  if (!person) {
1214	    return {
1215	      personDeleted: false,
1216	      factsDeleted: 0,
1217	      sourcesRedacted: 0,
1218	      orphanedAudioBlobUrls: [],
1219	    };
1220	  }
1221	
1222	  // 1. Delete every fact anchored to the person; remember affected sources.
1223	  const personFactFilter = { tenantId, "anchors.personId": personId };
1224	  const affectedSourceIds = await facts.distinct("sourceId", personFactFilter);
1225	  const { deletedCount: factsDeleted } = await facts.deleteMany(personFactFilter);
1226	
1227	  // 2. Discard pending fact drafts about the person in open proposals.
1228	  await proposals.updateMany(
1229	    { tenantId, status: "open" },
1230	    { $set: { "factDrafts.$[draft].resolution.status": "discarded" } },
1231	    { arrayFilters: [{ "draft.anchors.personId": personId }] }
1232	  );
1233	
1234	  // 3. Redact the person's identifiers wherever they appear in source text.
1235	  //    Redaction, not deletion: a source may cover other entities too.
1236	  const identifiers = [person.name, ...person.emails].filter(
1237	    (identifier) => identifier.length > 2
1238	  );
1239	  const pattern = new RegExp(identifiers.map(escapeRegex).join("|"), "gi");
1240	  const mentioningSources = await sources
1241	    .find({
1242	      tenantId,
1243	      $or: [
1244	        { content: { $regex: pattern } },
1245	        { "email.subject": { $regex: pattern } },
1246	        { "email.originalSender": { $regex: pattern } },
1247	      ],
1248	    })
1249	    .toArray();
1250	
1251	  for (const source of mentioningSources) {
1252	    await sources.updateOne(
1253	      { _id: source._id },
1254	      {
1255	        $set: {
1256	          ...(source.content
1257	            ? { content: source.content.replace(pattern, REDACTED) }
1258	            : {}),
1259	          ...(source.email
1260	            ? {
1261	                "email.subject": source.email.subject.replace(pattern, REDACTED),
1262	                "email.originalSender": pattern.test(source.email.originalSender)
1263	                  ? REDACTED
1264	                  : source.email.originalSender,
1265	              }
1266	            : {}),
1267	          updatedAt: new Date(),
1268	        },
1269	      }
1270	    );
1271	  }
1272	
1273	  // 4. Report audio blobs whose source no longer backs any fact — the caller
1274	  //    (app layer) deletes them from Vercel Blob.
1275	  const orphanedAudioBlobUrls: string[] = [];
1276	  for (const sourceId of affectedSourceIds) {
1277	    const remaining = await facts.countDocuments({ tenantId, sourceId });
1278	    if (remaining === 0) {
1279	      const source = await sources.findOne({ _id: sourceId, tenantId });
1280	      if (source?.audio) {
1281	        orphanedAudioBlobUrls.push(source.audio.blobUrl);
1282	      }
1283	    }
1284	  }
1285	
1286	  // 5. Delete the person document itself.
1287	  await people.deleteOne({ _id: personId, tenantId });
1288	
1289	  return {
1290	    personDeleted: true,
1291	    factsDeleted,
1292	    sourcesRedacted: mentioningSources.length,
1293	    orphanedAudioBlobUrls,
1294	  };
1295	};
1296	```
1297	
1298	Note on the `pattern.test` call: `RegExp.test` with the `g` flag is stateful (`lastIndex`). It is used exactly once per source on `originalSender`, after `.replace` calls that do not share state with `.test` — but to be safe from the reviewer's-eye view, `pattern.lastIndex = 0;` may be inserted before the `.test` call inside the loop. The test in Step 1 catches this class of bug (`originalSender` must equal `[REDACTED]`).

# MongoDB Connection Optimizer

You are an expert in MongoDB connection management across all officially supported driver languages (Node.js, Python, Java, Go, C#, Ruby, PHP, etc.). Your role is to ensure connection configurations are optimized for the user's specific environment and requirements, avoiding the common pitfall of blindly applying arbitrary parameters.

## Core Principle: Context Before Configuration

**NEVER add connection pool parameters or timeout settings without first understanding the application's context.** Arbitrary values without justification lead to performance issues and harder-to-debug problems.

## Understanding How Connection Pools Work

- Connection pooling exists because establishing a MongoDB connection is expensive (TCP + TLS + auth = 50-500ms). Without pooling, every operation pays this cost.
- Open connections consume system memory on the MongoDB server instances, ~1 MB per connection on average, even when they are not active. It is advised to avoid having idle connections.

**Connection Lifecycle**: Borrow from pool → Execute operation → Return to pool → Prune idle connections exceeding `maxIdleTimeMS`.

**Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Drivers**:
- **Synchronous** (PyMongo, Java sync): Thread blocks; pool size often matches thread pool size
- **Asynchronous** (Node.js, Motor): Non-blocking I/O; smaller pools suffice

**Monitoring Connections**: Each MongoClient establishes 2 monitoring connections per replica set member (automatic, separate from your pool). Formula: `Total = (minPoolSize + 2) × replica members × app instances`. Example: 10 instances, minPoolSize 5, 3-member set = 210 server connections. Always account for this when planning capacity.

## Configuration Design

**Before suggesting any configuration changes**, ensure you have the sufficient context about the user's application environment to inform pool configuration (see **Environmental Context** below). If you don't have enough information, ask targeted questions to gather it. Ask **only one question at a time**, starting with broad context (deployment type, workload, concurrency) before drilling down into specifics.

When you suggest configuration, briefly explain WHY each parameter has its specific value based on the context you gathered. Use the user's environment details (deployment type, workload, concurrency) to justify your recommendations.

Example: `maxPoolSize: 50` — "Based on your observed peak of 40 concurrent operations with 25% headroom for traffic bursts"

If you provide code snippets, add inline comments explaining the rationale for each parameter choice.

### Calculating Initial Pool Size

If performance data available: `Pool Size ≈ (Ops/sec) × (Avg duration) + 10-20% buffer`

Example: `(10,000 ops/sec) × (10ms) + 20% buffer = 120 connections`

Use when: Clear requirements, known latency, predictable traffic.
Don't use when: variable durations—start conservative (10-20), monitor, adjust.

Query optimization can dramatically reduce required pool size.

The total number of supported connections in a cluster could inform the upper limit of poolSize based on the number of MongoClient's instances employed. For example, if you have 10 instances of MongoClient using a size of 5 connecting to a 3 node replica set: `10 instances × 5 connections × 3 servers = 150 connections`. 

Each connection requires ~1 MB of physical RAM, so you may find that the optimal value for this parameter is also informed by the resource footprint of your application's workload.

#### The role of Topology:
- Pools are created per server per MongoClient. 
- By default, clients connect to one mongos router per sharded cluster (which manages connections to the shards internally), not to individual shards; so the shard amount do not affect the pool size directly.
- Shards share the workload and reduce stress on each individual server, increasing cluster capacity.
- Replica members do not affect the max pool directly. If the driver communicates with multiple replica set members (for example for reads with secondary read preference), it may create a pool per member.
- Replica set members do not increase write capacity (only the primary handles writes). However, they can increase read capacity if your application uses read preferences that allow secondary reads.

#### Server-Side Connection Limits: 
Total potential connections = instances × (maxPoolSize + 2) × replica set members. The + 2 accounts for the two monitoring connections per replica set member, per MongoClient instance. Monitor `connections.current` to avoid hitting limits. See `references/monitoring-guide.md` for how to set up monitoring.

**Self-managed Servers**: Set `net.maxIncomingConnections` to a value slightly higher than the maximum number of connections that the client creates, or the maximum size of the connection pool. This setting prevents the mongos from causing connection spikes on the individual shards that disrupt the operation and memory allocation of the sharded cluster.

### Configuration Scenarios

**General best practices:**

- Create client once only and reuse across application (in serverless, initialize outside handler)
- Don't manually close connections unless shutting down
- Max pool size must exceed expected concurrency
- Make use of timeouts to keep only the required connections ready as per your workload's needs
- Use default max pool size (100) unless you have specific needs (see scenarios below)

#### Scenario: Serverless Environments (Lambda, Cloud Functions)

**Critical pattern**: Initialize client OUTSIDE handler/function scope to enable connection reuse across warm invocations.

**Recommended configuration**:

| Parameter | Value | Reasoning |
|-----------|-------|-----------|
| `maxPoolSize` | 3-5 | Each serverless function instance has its own pool |
| `minPoolSize` | 0 | Prevent maintaining unused connections. Increase to mitigate cold starts if needed |
| `maxIdleTimeMS` | 10-30s | Release unused connections more quickly |
| `connectTimeoutMS` | >0 | Set to a value greater than the longest network latency you have to a member of the set |
| `socketTimeoutMS` | >0 | Use socketTimeoutMS to ensure that sockets are always closed |

##### Scenario: Traditional Long-Running Servers (OLTP Workload)

**Recommended configuration**:

| Parameter | Value | Reasoning |
|-----------|-------|-----------|
| `maxPoolSize` | 50+ | Based on peak concurrent requests (monitor and adjust) |
| `minPoolSize` | 10-20 | Pre-warmed connections ready for traffic spikes |
| `maxIdleTimeMS` | 5-10min | Stable servers benefit from persistent connections |
| `connectTimeoutMS` | 5-10s | Fail fast on connection issues |
| `socketTimeoutMS` | 30s | Prevent hanging queries; appropriate for short OLTP operations |
| `serverSelectionTimeoutMS` | 5s | Quick failover for replica set topology changes |

MongoDB 8.0+ introduces defaultMaxTimeMS on Atlas clusters, which provides server-side protection against long-running operations.

##### Scenario: OLAP / Analytical Workloads

**Recommended configuration**:

| Parameter | Value | Reasoning |
|-----------|-------|-----------|
| `maxPoolSize` | 10-20 | Fewer concurrent operations. Match your expected concurrent analytical operations |
| `minPoolSize` | 0-5 | Queries are infrequent; minimal pre-warming needed |
| `socketTimeoutMS` | >0 | Set socketTimeoutMS to two or three times the length of the slowest operation that the driver runs. |
| `maxIdleTimeMS` | 10min | Minimize connection churn while not keeping truly idle connections too long. Consider the timeouts of intermediate network devices |

##### Scenario: High-Traffic / Bursty Workloads

**Recommended configuration**:

| Parameter | Value | Reasoning |
|-----------|-------|-----------|
| `maxPoolSize` | 100+ | Higher ceiling to accommodate sudden traffic spikes |
| `minPoolSize` | 20-30 | More pre-warmed connections ready for immediate bursts |
| `maxConnecting` | 2 (default) | Prevent thundering herd during sudden demand |
| `waitQueueTimeoutMS` | 2-5s | Fail fast when pool exhausted rather than queueing indefinitely |
| `maxIdleTimeMS` | 5min | Balance between reuse during bursts and cleanup between spikes |

## Troubleshooting Connection Issues
If the user requires help to troubleshoot connection issues, determine whether this is a client config issue or infrastructure problem.

Types of issues:

- **Infrastructure or Network Issues (Out of Scope)**: redirect to publicly available infractructure documentation.
  - eg: DNS/SRV resolution failures, network/VPC blocking, IP not whitelisted, TLS cert issues, auth mechanism mismatches
- **Client Configuration Issues (Your Territory)**:
  - eg: Pool exhaustion, inappropriate timeouts, poor reuse patterns, suboptimal sizing, missing serverless caching, connection churn

### Guidelines
- Ask **only one question at a time**, starting with broad context (deployment type, workload, concurrency) before drilling down into specifics (current config, error messages). This approach allows you to quickly narrow down the root cause and avoid unnecessary configuration changes or excessive questions.
- Review `references/monitoring-guide.md` for how to instrument and monitor the relevant parameters that can inform your troubleshooting and recommendations.

### Pool Exhaustion
When operations queue, pool is exhausted.

**Symptoms**: `MongoWaitQueueTimeoutError`, `WaitQueueTimeoutError` or `MongoTimeoutException`, increased latency, operations waiting.

**Solutions**:
- **Increase `maxPoolSize`** when: Wait queue has operations waiting (size > 0) + server shows low utilization
- **Don't increase** when: Server is at capacity. Suggest query optimization.

### Connection Timeouts (ECONNREFUSED, SocketTimeout)

**Client Solutions**: Increase `connectTimeoutMS`/`socketTimeoutMS` if legitimately needed

**Infrastructure Issues** (redirect): 
- Cannot connect via shell: Network/firewall; 
- Environment-specific: VPC/security; 
- DNS errors: DNS/SRV resolution

### Connection Churn
**Symptoms**: Rapidly increasing `connections.totalCreated` server metric, high connection handling CPU

**Causes**: Not using pooling, not caching in serverless, `maxIdleTimeMS` too low, restart loops

### High Latency
- Ensure `minPoolSize` > 0 for traffic spikes
- Network compression for high-latency (>50ms): `compressors: ['snappy', 'zlib']`
- Nearest read preference for geo-distributed setups

---
## Environmental Context (MANDATORY)

**ALWAYS** verify you have the sufficient context about the user's application environment to inform pool configuration BEFORE suggesting any configuration changes.

### Parameters that inform a pool configuration
- **Server's memory limits**: each connection takes 1MB against the server.
- **Number of clients and servers in a cluster**: pools are per client and per server, taking memory from the cluster.
- **OLAP vs OLTP**: timeout values must support the expected duration of operations.
  - Expected duration of operations: Short OLTP queries may require lower socketTimeoutMS to fail fast on hanging operations, while long-running OLAP queries may need higher values to avoid premature timeouts.
- **Server version**: MongoDB 8.0+ also introduces defaultMaxTimeMS on Atlas clusters, which provides server-side protection against long-running operations.
- **Serverless vs Traditional**: Serverless functions should initialize clients outside the handler to enable connection reuse across warm invocations, while traditional servers can maintain larger pools with pre-warmed connections.
- **Concurrency and traffic patterns**: High concurrency and bursty traffic may require larger pools and more pre-warmed connections, while steady, low-concurrency workloads can often operate efficiently with smaller pools.
-  **Operating System**: Some OSes have limits on the number of open file descriptors, which can impact the maximum number of connections. It's important to consider these limits when configuring connection pools, especially for high-traffic applications.
- **Driver version**: Different driver versions may have different default settings and performance characteristics. Always check the documentation for the specific driver version being used to ensure optimal configuration.

**Guidelines:**
- Ask only questions relevant to the scenarios in **Configuration Design Phase**. Omit questions that won't lead to a clear use of the content in **Configuration Design Phase**.
- If an answer not provided, make a reasonable assumption and disclose it.

---

## Advising on Monitoring & Iteration

**You must guide users to monitor** the relevant parameters to their pool configuration. 
For detailed monitoring setup, see `references/monitoring-guide.md`.

---

## When creating code
For every connection parameter you provide (in recommendations or code snippets), ensure you have enough context about the user's application environment to inform values. If not, ask targeted questions before suggesting specific values. If you get no answer, make a reasonable assumption, disclose it and comment the relevant parameters accordingly in the code.

content.thinking:
Looking at the test results, I'm seeing 20 passing tests with 12 skipped due to the missing MongoDB test URI, which totals 32 tests. The PR mentioned 28 passing tests in the integration environment (22 unit + 6 integration), so the discrepancy seems to come from how tests are counted depending on whether the environment variable is set.

The integration tests won't run without a local MongoDB instance, and I could spin up Docker to run them, but that's low priority since the PR already showed those tests passing and the code hasn't changed. I'll skip that for now.

While waiting for the agent results, I'm organizing my own review findings. I've identified that the PR conflicts with main because both branches have the same root fixes, so a rebase would clean that up. There's also an unrelated commit in the PR that I can mention but doesn't need to be removed.

For the code itself, I'm seeing a few candidate issues. The client.ts file lacks connection options for serverless environments—things like maxPoolSize, maxIdleTimeMS, and timeouts—which is a proposal rather than a bug, though Atlas connection caps make the defaults risky long-term. On the search.ts side, there's a question about filter placement: moving the lifecycle exclusion into the $search stage via mustNot exists would require updating index mappings, and while it might improve scoring and prepare for $rankFusion, the current approach of filtering after $search actually works correctly for getting accurate top-K results.

I'm also noting a gap around entity-name search—the spec calls for fuzzy entity matching in the resolve and search steps, which isn't implemented yet but should be scheduled for Plan 2 rather than treated as a Plan-1 defect. And there's an under-redaction issue where only full person names are matched, so first-name-only mentions in transcripts slip through.

For the name-matching problem, I'm thinking about tokenizing names by whitespace and redacting tokens that are at least 3 characters with word boundaries, accepting some over-redaction to be safe—though I need to be careful with common short tokens. This is a GDPR-relevant improvement worth flagging as medium priority.

There's also a persistence issue with orphaned blob URLs: if the caller crashes before deleting blobs, a re-run of erasePerson returns early since the person is already gone, leaving audio with the erased person's voice still in Blob storage.  I should add a flag like `audioPendingDeletion` or `audio.deletedAt` to track this within the cascade so callers can sweep by that flag—medium priority for the GDPR audit trail.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/eric/.claude/skills/merging-branches-safely

# Merging Branches Safely

## Overview

Investigate merges **before** touching the working tree. Use `git merge-tree` to predict conflicts without mutating state, classify each conflict, surface a resolution proposal, and only run `git merge` / `git rebase` after the user approves — or immediately if preflight predicts no conflicts.

**Core primitive:** `git merge-tree A B` simulates a full merge and prints conflict markers. No index, worktree, or HEAD changes. It is the single most important tool in this skill.

**Announce at start:** "Using merging-branches-safely — starting with read-only preflight."

## The Four Phases

```dot
digraph merge_flow {
    preflight [shape=box, label="Phase 1: Preflight (read-only)"];
    predicted [shape=diamond, label="merge-tree predicts conflicts?"];
    classify [shape=box, label="Phase 2: Classify + propose"];
    approved [shape=diamond, label="User approves resolution?"];
    execute [shape=box, label="Phase 3: Execute merge/rebase\n+ verify"];
    commit [shape=box, label="Phase 4: Commit (no push)"];
    revise [shape=box, label="Revise proposal"];

    preflight -> predicted;
    predicted -> classify [label="yes"];
    predicted -> execute [label="no"];
    classify -> approved;
    approved -> revise [label="no"];
    revise -> classify;
    approved -> execute [label="yes"];
    execute -> commit;
}
```

### Phase 1 — Preflight (ALWAYS, read-only)

Never start a merge/rebase before this phase completes. Collect, without mutating state:

```bash
# Fork point
BASE=$(git merge-base <ours> <theirs>)

# What each side added
git log --oneline <theirs> ^<ours>          # incoming commits
git log --oneline <ours> ^<theirs>          # our commits

# File-level scope
git diff --stat $BASE..<ours>
git diff --stat $BASE..<theirs>

# Overlap set — files touched on both sides
comm -12 \
  <(git diff --name-only $BASE..<ours> | sort) \
  <(git diff --name-only $BASE..<theirs> | sort)

# Conflict prediction (merge)
git merge-tree <ours> <theirs> 2>&1 | grep -E "^CONFLICT|^Auto-merging"

# Conflict prediction (rebase) — simulate each commit replaying
for sha in $(git log --reverse --format=%H $BASE..<theirs>); do
  git merge-tree <ours> $sha | grep "^CONFLICT" && echo "  ^ at $sha"
done
```

Report to the user: incoming commits, scope, overlap, predicted conflicts (or "none").

If no conflicts predicted → skip to Phase 3.

### Phase 2 — Classify + propose (only when conflicts predicted)

For every overlapping file (conflicting **and** auto-merging), inspect both sides' diffs:

```bash
git diff $BASE..<ours>   -- <path>
git diff $BASE..<theirs> -- <path>
```

Tag each file with one of:

| Tag | Meaning | Default resolution |
|---|---|---|
| `orthogonal` | Both sides edit the same region with semantically independent changes (e.g., one adds an import, one adds a different import nearby) | Combine both |
| `supersede` | One side's change replaces the other's intent (e.g., feature deleted a function main renamed) | Take the winning side and justify |
| `semantic-overlap` | Both sides modify the same behavior — no mechanical answer | Escalate: present options, let user pick |
| `silent-semantic` | Git reports a **clean auto-merge** but the combined code is broken (renamed identifier still referenced, type contract mismatched, invariant violated) | Flag and propose fix — these are the dangerous ones |
| `generated-artifact` | A conflict in a file produced from source, not hand-authored — `pnpm-lock.yaml`, other lockfiles, generated schemas/types | Don't resolve the artifact. Resolve its **source** (the `package.json` files), then **regenerate** it — see Phase 3 |

Auto-merged files still need a classification. `silent-semantic` only surfaces if you look. Skipping this check is the most common failure mode.

**Stop and ask.** Present:
- Per-file tag + proposed resolution (one line each)
- Any `silent-semantic` flags prominently
- A single "approve / change / abort" question

Wait for approval. Do not start the merge.

### Phase 3 — Execute (only after approval, or immediately if Phase 1 was clean)

```bash
git merge <theirs> --no-commit --no-ff   # or: git rebase <theirs>
```

For each conflicting file, apply the approved resolution with the Edit tool (not by hand-rewriting full files).

**`pnpm-lock.yaml` (and any `generated-artifact`) is the exception — never Edit it.** It is generated from the `package.json` files. Resolve every conflicting `package.json` first, **merging both sides' intent** — main's dependency changes *and* the branch's — not one side wholesale. Then discard the conflicted lockfile and regenerate it:

```bash
# Pick the lockfile side that has been re-resolved more recently:
#   merge (main into branch): git checkout --theirs  → uses main's lockfile
#   rebase (branch onto main): git checkout --ours   → also main's lockfile (rebase inverts the semantics)
# Either way, you want main's transitive baseline — Renovate keeps it fresh.
git checkout --theirs pnpm-lock.yaml
pnpm install --lockfile-only --recursive --ignore-scripts --ignore-pnpmfile
pnpm dedupe --ignore-scripts         # only if the repo dedupes its lockfile (check renovate.json5 postUpdateOptions)
git add pnpm-lock.yaml
```

**Side choice matters.** `pnpm install --lockfile-only` is conservative — it keeps every transitive resolution that still satisfies the merged manifests' ranges. If the *branch* side is stale, its older (sometimes vulnerable) transitives still satisfy the caret ranges, so they survive regen + dedupe. Starting from main's lockfile gives pnpm the freshest baseline to reconcile against. `pnpm dedupe` consolidates duplicates but **does not** upgrade resolutions — it cannot fix this on its own. OSV scans on the PR will surface the resulting vulnerability delta against main if you pick the wrong side.

For the full command matrix — lockfile-only-update PRs, `lockFileMaintenance` PRs, the verify-the-bump-landed grep — see `rebasing-renovate-prs-locally`, the specialization for when the whole PR *is* a dependency bump.

Then:

```bash
# Re-verify no markers remain
grep -rn "^<<<<<<< \|^======= $\|^>>>>>>> " <touched-paths>

# Also open each auto-merged overlap file and confirm semantics
# (silent-semantic hides here — auto-merge being clean is not a safety check)

# Run project verification
<project-typecheck-command>
<project-test-command-if-user-has-that-convention>

# If the merge touched package.json / pnpm-lock.yaml: typecheck + test are NOT enough.
# A re-resolved dependency tree can break the bundler only. Also run:
<project-build-command>
pnpm deps:lint                       # syncpack — catches override/specifier drift
```

If verification fails, fix before committing. Never `--no-verify` to ship a broken merge.

### Phase 4 — Commit (never push)

```bash
git add <resolved-paths>
git commit --no-edit          # merge message pre-filled; rebase: git rebase --continue
```

Stop here. Pushing is a separate user-authorized action.

## Guardrails

- **Never `git merge --abort` as an exploration tool.** That's what `git merge-tree` is for. Aborting after a partial merge loses signal and adds noise to the reflog.
- **Never start a merge/rebase before Phase 1.**
- **Never use `-X ours`, `-X theirs`, or `--no-verify` to skip resolution.** They hide conflicts; they don't resolve them.
- **Dirty working tree at Phase 1 → stop and surface.** Do not stash silently; the user may have in-progress work.
- **Auto-merge clean ≠ semantically clean.** Every overlap file gets a tag, including auto-merged ones.
- **Never Edit `pnpm-lock.yaml` (or any generated artifact) to resolve a conflict.** It's derived from the manifests — fix those, then regenerate. A hand-merged lockfile drifts from what the resolver produces and breaks `--frozen-lockfile` installs.
- **One tag per file, written down.** Forces naming before fixing.
- **The approval gate is bypassable in two cases:** (1) Phase 1 predicts zero conflicts, or (2) the user has given explicit pre-authorization in this turn (e.g., "merge and commit, no need to confirm"). Absent either, pause. A generic "merge X into Y" does not count as pre-authorization — users often expect to see the preflight before resolution begins.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why it fails | Do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Running `git merge` to "see what conflicts" | Mutates state; forces `--abort`; pollutes reflog | Use `git merge-tree` — zero side effects |
| Skipping auto-merged files in Phase 2 | `silent-semantic` conflicts hide here | Every overlap file gets a tag |
| Resolving before user approval | Treats "merge branch X" as resolution authorization | Approval gate is mandatory when conflicts are predicted |
| Inferring conflict type from the conflict markers alone | Markers show syntax, not intent — you need each side's diff from the merge base | `git diff $BASE..<ours> -- <path>` and the same for theirs |
| Skipping typecheck/tests before commit | Leaves broken merges as commits | Run the project's verification command; if it fails, fix before committing |
| Hand-resolving `pnpm-lock.yaml` conflict markers | Produces a lockfile no resolver would generate; `--frozen-lockfile` installs break | Resolve the `package.json` files, then regenerate the lockfile (Phase 3) |
| Only typecheck/test after a dep-touching merge | Bundler-only breakage (missing transitive export, etc.) passes both | Also run the build + `pnpm deps:lint` when the merge changed dependencies |
| Pushing after committing | User didn't ask for that | Stop at Phase 4; push is a separate ask |

## Quick Reference

**Merge command recipe (after approval):**
```bash
git merge main --no-commit --no-ff
# ... apply per-file resolutions via Edit tool ...
# pnpm-lock.yaml: do NOT Edit — resolve the package.json files, then regenerate (Phase 3)
grep -rn '^<<<<<<< \|^>>>>>>> ' <touched-paths>   # expect no output
<typecheck>   # + build & pnpm deps:lint if deps changed
git add <resolved-paths>
git commit --no-edit
```

**Rebase recipe (after approval):**
```bash
git rebase <target>
# per commit that conflicts:
#   - apply resolution via Edit
#   - git add <paths>
#   - git rebase --continue
<typecheck>   # after the whole rebase finishes
```

**Resuming an in-progress merge you didn't start:** treat the current state as mid-Phase-3. Run `git status` to find unmerged paths, then loop back to Phase 2 on those files: read each side's diff from merge base, tag, propose, wait for approval — don't resolve blind.

## Red Flags — Stop and Restart the Phase

- About to run `git merge` / `git rebase` without having run `git merge-tree` → back to Phase 1
- About to resolve conflicts without having surfaced tags + proposal → back to Phase 2
- Auto-merged file not classified → back to Phase 2
- About to commit without running project verification → back to Phase 3
- About to Edit `pnpm-lock.yaml` or another generated artifact to clear conflict markers → stop; resolve its source and regenerate (Phase 3)
- About to push → stop; that's not this skill's job

# MongoDB Atlas capability check — verified 2026-07-31

## 1. $rankFusion / $scoreFusion / "$rank"

**Findings:**
- **$rankFusion: GA.** Shipped GA in server 8.1 (released 2025-06-30); usable on 8.0.x only by opening a support case (feature-flag enablement). Docs: "$rankFusion is only available for deployments that use MongoDB 8.0 and later. You must open a support case to use $rankFusion on 8.0.X versions." $vectorSearch inside input pipelines requires 8.1+. Must be first stage; sub-pipelines limited to $search/$vectorSearch/$match/$sort/$geoNear; no views-in-definition, no time series, no pagination, sub-pipelines run serially.
  - https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/rankfusion/ (current 8.3 manual)
  - https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/product-release-announcements/boost-search-relevance-mongodb-atlas-native-hybrid-search (posted 2025-06-25, updated 2026-06-30: "Hybrid search is generally available, including $rankFusion for clusters on 8.0+ and $scoreFusion on clusters on 8.2+")
- **$scoreFusion: GA.** Public preview in 8.2 (2025-09-30), GA in 8.3 (2026-05-31). Current docs instruct: "To use $scoreFusion, your cluster must run MongoDB v8.3 or later."
  - https://www.mongodb.com/products/updates/public-preview-mongodb-native-hybrid-search-with-scorefusion/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/hybrid-search/hybrid-search/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/scorefusion/
- **Tiers:** these are server stages, no Search Nodes dependency. But M0/Flex clusters are pinned to 8.0 (see Q5), and 8.0.x needs a support case for $rankFusion — so on M0/Flex treat $rankFusion as **effectively unavailable** (no doc says Atlas enabled the flag fleet-wide there — UNCONFIRMED either way). On M10+ it requires choosing "Latest Version With Auto Upgrades" (8.3) or a support case on 8.0.
- **No new stage literally called `$rank` exists.** `$rank` remains the window operator inside $setWindowFields (since 5.0). What the user heard is almost certainly **$rankFusion** (hybrid-search GA marketing, June 2025/2026) — or possibly the brand-new **$rerank** (2026-06-30, see Q4). Related new scoring stage: **$score** (normalize/compute score metadata, in 8.3 manual; arrived with the 8.2/8.3 hybrid-scoring work): https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/score

**Impact on our design:** None negative — our BM25-only design doesn't use them; if we ever add hybrid search we need a dedicated M10+ on "Latest Version With Auto Upgrades" (8.3), not Flex/M0.

## 2. Automated Embedding in Atlas Vector Search — THE DECIDING FACTOR

**Findings:**
- **Status: Public Preview on Atlas since 2026-05-07/11** (products update May 7; blog May 11). Not GA as of 2026-07-31. Index type `autoEmbed`, query via `$vectorSearch.query` text. Supported on M0, Flex, M10+ (M10+ requires storage AND compute auto-scaling enabled, max tier ≥ M30). Also public preview for self-managed Community Edition 8.2+ (uses your own Voyage API key; text goes to api.voyageai.com).
  - https://www.mongodb.com/products/updates/now-in-public-preview-automated-embedding-in-mongodb-vector-search-on-atlas/ (2026-05-07)
  - https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/product-release-announcements/ai-search-for-agents-announcing-automated-embedding-atlas (2026-05-11)
  - https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/crud-embeddings/automated-embedding/
- **WHERE INFERENCE RUNS — verbatim from current docs** (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/vector-search-type — Index Limitations section): "The embedding model inference runs on a multi-tenant service in the Atlas Data Plane, available in **MongoDB's Google Cloud based infrastructure in a US region**. This means that your data is **sent to MongoDB's inference infrastructure** for embedding generation and retrieval, **regardless of your cluster's cloud provider**. Data transfer costs apply." Corroborated by https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/crud-embeddings/automated-embedding/overview ("The model inference platform runs on MongoDB's infrastructure in Google Cloud cloud in a US region"). Text is not stored or used for training; TLS in transit; embeddings persist in an internal collection (`__mdb_internal_search`) on your own cluster.
- **No EU region option exists or is announced.** I searched MongoDB blog, products/updates, and docs for any 2026 EU/regional-inference announcement: nothing. UNCONFIRMED only in the sense that no roadmap statement exists either way.
- Models: voyage-4-lite $0.02 / voyage-4 $0.06 / voyage-4-large $0.12 / voyage-code-3 $0.18 per 1M tokens; 32k context; one-time 200M free tokens per model per org. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/crud-embeddings/automated-embedding/models
- Governance note: Atlas Resource Policies can forbid `autoEmbed` index creation org-wide (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-resource-policies) — worth enabling for this client to prevent accidental use.

**Impact on our design: the 2026-07-10 rejection stands, now with an exact citation.** Your spec said "Google-US" — docs now literally confirm "Google Cloud … US region, regardless of your cluster's cloud provider." Raw `facts.text` would leave Frankfurt. Do not enable autoEmbed; optionally add a resource policy forbidding it.

## 3. Voyage AI API (EU endpoint / DPA)

**Findings:**
- The standalone Voyage API is being migrated to the **Atlas "Embedding and Reranking API"** at `https://ai.mongodb.com/v1/*` — **Public Preview since 2026-01-15**, keys managed in Atlas ("model API keys"), 200M free tokens on latest models, explicitly "not for production" during preview. Old api.voyageai.com endpoints map 1:1 to ai.mongodb.com. Launched together with the **voyage-4 model family** (shared embedding space across 4-series).
  - https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/product-release-announcements/introducing-the-embedding-and-reranking-api-on-mongodb-atlas (2026-01-15)
  - https://www.mongodb.com/docs/voyageai/tutorials/migrate-to-atlas ; https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/02/mongodb-embedding-reranking-api (2026-02)
- **No EU endpoint, no EU data-residency option, no region selection documented** for ai.mongodb.com or api.voyageai.com. No Voyage-specific EU DPA found. Third-party assessments in 2026 describe Voyage's residency posture as immature vs. Cohere/Mistral. Hosting region of ai.mongodb.com: not explicitly documented — **UNCONFIRMED**, but the only documented Voyage serving infrastructure (the Atlas inference platform, Q2) is US/Google Cloud; assume US processing.
- **In-your-own-cloud options grew** (these ARE EU-capable because you pick the region and the model runs in your account): AWS Marketplace/SageMaker model packages ("Deploy models in your account and VPC… AWS serves as your sub-processor") — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/voyageai/management/aws-marketplace ; **Azure AI Foundry** — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/voyageai/management/azure-foundry ; **Google Cloud Model Garden** — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/voyageai/management/gcp-marketplace. No Atlas-calls-Voyage-in-region integration exists; $vectorSearch/autoEmbed cannot point at your own SageMaker endpoint.

**Impact on our design:** Fallback plan unchanged and slightly better: Mistral embed (EU) or self-deployed Voyage via SageMaker eu-central-1 / Azure AI Foundry EU — both keep data in-region under your DPA with the hyperscaler. The hosted Voyage API remains a US processor and is also formally "preview, not for production."

## 4. Atlas Search / Vector Search platform changes since mid-2025

Source: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/search-changelog/ (entries dated as listed)

- **2026-06-30: Native Reranking — new `$rerank` aggregation stage** (Voyage rerank models). **Preview**, Atlas-only, requires MongoDB 8.3+ ("Latest Version With Auto Upgrades"), opt-in per project (Project Settings toggle + cost acknowledgment), not available self-managed/Atlas Local. Docs state "$rerank does not run Voyage AI reranking models on your Atlas cluster resources" — inference is external (same MongoDB-hosted model platform; region not stated, assume US — UNCONFIRMED explicitly). Pricing rerank-2.5 $0.05/1M, rerank-2.5-lite $0.02/1M, 200M free tokens. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/query/aggregation-stages/rerank/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/voyageai/models/rerankers
- **German-language relevant: 2025-07-10 release changed the `german` stemmer's umlaut handling (ä/ö/ü → ae/oe/ue) and marked `german2` outdated.** If our `facts.text` field uses `lucene.german`, match behavior changed mid-2025; verify recall on umlaut terms after any reindex.
- **Facets:** `stringFacet`/`numberFacet`/`dateFacet` index types are "outdated" — replaced by faceting directly on `token`/`number`/`date` types (2025-01-24, 2025-06-10). `token` faceting is the recommended path, NOT deprecated. Facet bucket limits raised to 10,000 (2026-05-25 strings, 2026-06-24 numbers/dates). Multi-select faceting added 2026-04-14.
- **Not deprecated, still standard:** `dynamic: false` static mappings (still the documented performance recommendation) and the `compound.filter` pattern. No breaking changes to `$search` operators we use.
- **Breaking-ish:** from server 8.0.14 (2025-09-25 release note), `returnStoredSource`/`scoreDetails` must be boolean; passing `null` now errors.
- Other additions: `typeSets` dynamic-indexing config + `stableTfl`/`boolean` similarities (2025-09-25); `returnScope`, `hasRoot`, `hasAncestor` for array-of-objects querying (2025-10-21); lexical prefilters for the `vectorSearch` operator (preview, 2025-11-24); index-field-limit alerts (2026-01-29); flat vector indexes for multitenant workloads (preview, 2026-04-07); `storedSource` on vector indexes (2026-04-27); `$vectorSearch` over arrays of embeddings (preview, 2026-04-30); index-time sorted indexes + `englishMinimalStemming` (2026-07-06).
- **Tier limits (current):** M0 = max **3** search indexes total (search+vector), Flex = **10**; index definition ≤3KB, ≤300 fields, 1 synonym mapping on those tiers; cluster-wide hard cap 2,500. M2/M5 shared tiers are gone (migrated to Flex). https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/deployment/feature-compatibility
- **Search Nodes in Frankfurt: yes** — AWS `eu-central-1` (EU_CENTRAL_1) is in the dedicated-Search-Nodes region table; M10+ only (never M0/Flex); cheapest S10 tier is AWS-only. Not required for anything we do. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/amazon-aws
- **Rebranding:** "Atlas Search"/"Atlas Vector Search" are now "MongoDB Search"/"MongoDB Vector Search" with new doc sites (mongodb.com/docs/search/, /docs/vector-search/); search also runs on Community Edition 8.2+ self-managed. Old /docs/atlas/atlas-search URLs redirect.

**Impact on our design:** Nothing we use is deprecated (`dynamic:false`, `compound.filter`, token facets all fine). Action items: check the German stemmer change against our analyzer choice, and note $rerank as a future quality lever that is currently preview + US-inference (same GDPR objection as Q2).

## 5. MongoDB versions on Atlas, July 2026

- Release train: 8.0 LTS (2024-10-31, supported to 2029-10-31) → rapid releases 8.1 (2025-06-30), 8.2 (2025-09-30), **8.3 = current latest (2026-05-31**, 8.3.7 as of 2026-07-24). **No 9.0 yet**; docs carry a "9.0 (Upcoming)" label; majors are ~yearly so expect fall 2026 — no announced date (UNCONFIRMED). https://endoflife.date/mongodb ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/release-notes/8.3/
- New dedicated (M10+) clusters choose: **7.0, 8.0, or "Latest Version With Auto Upgrades" (currently 8.3)**. You cannot pin 8.1/8.2/8.3 specifically; leaving auto-upgrades means you can only step back to a major in the 9.0→9.1 window. **Free (M0) and Flex are pinned to MongoDB 8.0** and auto-upgraded by Atlas. UI-preselected default not documented; the default major is 8.0. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-versions
- Practical stage floor: on M0/Flex assume an 8.0 feature set (no self-serve $rankFusion, no $scoreFusion, no $rerank). On M10+ with auto-upgrades: full 8.3 set.

**Impact on our design:** If the MVP is on Flex/M0, we are on 8.0 — plain `$search` BM25 is fully supported there and that's all we need. Any hybrid/rerank ambition implies M10+ with auto-upgrades.

## 6. Other 2026 items worth knowing

- **Voyage 4 family + voyage-context-4** (contextualized chunk embeddings) GA'd via the API in the 2026-01-15 announcement wave (PR: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/mongodb-sets-a-new-standard-for-retrieval-accuracy-with-voyage-4-models-for-production-ready-ai-applications-302662558.html). All 4-series models share one embedding space (mix models later without reindexing).
- **Atlas Resource Policies** now cover search/AI governance: forbid `autoEmbed` indexes, restrict the Embedding/Reranking API, restrict clusters to specific regions — a cheap, auditable GDPR guardrail for this project (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-resource-policies ; blog https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/innovation/enforce-data-sovereignty-with-mongodb-atlas-resource-policies).
- Automated Embedding on M10+ force-requires auto-scaling (to ≥M30 during initial index builds) — hidden cost trap for small consultancy budgets if anyone ever flips it on.
- Preview-feature terms apply to autoEmbed / $rerank / ai.mongodb.com: "might change at any time… do not use in production" — an independent reason (besides GDPR) they're out of scope for a client deliverable right now.

## Bottom line for the 2026-07-10 design

1. **Decision "reject auto-embedding, stay lexical" remains correct and is now explicitly documented by MongoDB**: inference is multi-tenant, Google Cloud, US region, regardless of cluster region.
2. **No EU path exists** for MongoDB-hosted Voyage inference (autoEmbed, $rerank, ai.mongodb.com) as of 2026-07-31 — GA'ing any of them won't fix residency; watch for a regional-inference announcement before revisiting.
3. **Embedding fallbacks unchanged**: Mistral (EU API) or self-deployed Voyage (SageMaker eu-central-1, now also Azure AI Foundry / GCP Model Garden in EU regions).
4. **One real action item**: verify the July 2025 `german` stemmer umlaut change against our analyzer configuration.
5. Nothing in our index definition pattern (dynamic:false, compound.filter, token facets) is deprecated; M0=3 / Flex=10 index limits and the 8.0 pin on those tiers are the only constraints to respect.</result>

## 4. Atlas Search / Vector Search platform changes since mid-2025

Source: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/search-changelog/ (entries dated as listed)

- **2026-06-30: Native Reranking — new `$rerank` aggregation stage** (Voyage rerank models). **Preview**, Atlas-only, requires MongoDB 8.3+ ("Latest Version With Auto Upgrades"), opt-in per project (Project Settings toggle + cost acknowledgment), not available self-managed/Atlas Local. Docs state "$rerank does not run Voyage AI reranking models on your Atlas cluster resources" — inference is external (same MongoDB-hosted model platform; region not stated, assume US — UNCONFIRMED explicitly). Pricing rerank-2.5 $0.05/1M, rerank-2.5-lite $0.02/1M, 200M free tokens. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/query/aggregation-stages/rerank/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/voyageai/models/rerankers
- **German-language relevant: 2025-07-10 release changed the `german` stemmer's umlaut handling (ä/ö/ü → ae/oe/ue) and marked `german2` outdated.** If our `facts.text` field uses `lucene.german`, match behavior changed mid-2025; verify recall on umlaut terms after any reindex.
- **Facets:** `stringFacet`/`numberFacet`/`dateFacet` index types are "outdated" — replaced by faceting directly on `token`/`number`/`date` types (2025-01-24, 2025-06-10). `token` faceting is the recommended path, NOT deprecated. Facet bucket limits raised to 10,000 (2026-05-25 strings, 2026-06-24 numbers/dates). Multi-select faceting added 2026-04-14.
- **Not deprecated, still standard:** `dynamic: false` static mappings (still the documented performance recommendation) and the `compound.filter` pattern. No breaking changes to `$search` operators we use.
- **Breaking-ish:** from server 8.0.14 (2025-09-25 release note), `returnStoredSource`/`scoreDetails` must be boolean; passing `null` now errors.
- Other additions: `typeSets` dynamic-indexing config + `stableTfl`/`boolean` similarities (2025-09-25); `returnScope`, `hasRoot`, `hasAncestor` for array-of-objects querying (2025-10-21); lexical prefilters for the `vectorSearch` operator (preview, 2025-11-24); index-field-limit alerts (2026-01-29); flat vector indexes for multitenant workloads (preview, 2026-04-07); `storedSource` on vector indexes (2026-04-27); `$vectorSearch` over arrays of embeddings (preview, 2026-04-30); index-time sorted indexes + `englishMinimalStemming` (2026-07-06).
- **Tier limits (current):** M0 = max **3** search indexes total (search+vector), Flex = **10**; index definition ≤3KB, ≤300 fields, 1 synonym mapping on those tiers; cluster-wide hard cap 2,500. M2/M5 shared tiers are gone (migrated to Flex). https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/deployment/feature-compatibility
- **Search Nodes in Frankfurt: yes** — AWS `eu-central-1` (EU_CENTRAL_1) is in the dedicated-Search-Nodes region table; M10+ only (never M0/Flex); cheapest S10 tier is AWS-only. Not required for anything we do. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/amazon-aws
- **Rebranding:** "Atlas Search"/"Atlas Vector Search" are now "MongoDB Search"/"MongoDB Vector Search" with new doc sites (mongodb.com/docs/search/, /docs/vector-search/); search also runs on Community Edition 8.2+ self-managed. Old /docs/atlas/atlas-search URLs redirect.

**Impact on our design:** Nothing we use is deprecated (`dynamic:false`, `compound.filter`, token facets all fine). Action items: check the German stemmer change against our analyzer choice, and note $rerank as a future quality lever that is currently preview + US-inference (same GDPR objection as Q2).

## 5. MongoDB versions on Atlas, July 2026

- Release train: 8.0 LTS (2024-10-31, supported to 2029-10-31) → rapid releases 8.1 (2025-06-30), 8.2 (2025-09-30), **8.3 = current latest (2026-05-31**, 8.3.7 as of 2026-07-24). **No 9.0 yet**; docs carry a "9.0 (Upcoming)" label; majors are ~yearly so expect fall 2026 — no announced date (UNCONFIRMED). https://endoflife.date/mongodb ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/release-notes/8.3/
- New dedicated (M10+) clusters choose: **7.0, 8.0, or "Latest Version With Auto Upgrades" (currently 8.3)**. You cannot pin 8.1/8.2/8.3 specifically; leaving auto-upgrades means you can only step back to a major in the 9.0→9.1 window. **Free (M0) and Flex are pinned to MongoDB 8.0** and auto-upgraded by Atlas. UI-preselected default not documented; the default major is 8.0. https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-versions
- Practical stage floor: on M0/Flex assume an 8.0 feature set (no self-serve $rankFusion, no $scoreFusion, no $rerank). On M10+ with auto-upgrades: full 8.3 set.

**Impact on our design:** If the MVP is on Flex/M0, we are on 8.0 — plain `$search` BM25 is fully supported there and that's all we need. Any hybrid/rerank ambition implies M10+ with auto-upgrades.

## 6. Other 2026 items worth knowing

- **Voyage 4 family + voyage-context-4** (contextualized chunk embeddings) GA'd via the API in the 2026-01-15 announcement wave (PR: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/mongodb-sets-a-new-standard-for-retrieval-accuracy-with-voyage-4-models-for-production-ready-ai-applications-302662558.html). All 4-series models share one embedding space (mix models later without reindexing).
- **Atlas Resource Policies** now cover search/AI governance: forbid `autoEmbed` indexes, restrict the Embedding/Reranking API, restrict clusters to specific regions — a cheap, auditable GDPR guardrail for this project (https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-resource-policies ; blog https://www.mongodb.com/company/blog/innovation/enforce-data-sovereignty-with-mongodb-atlas-resource-policies).
- Automated Embedding on M10+ force-requires auto-scaling (to ≥M30 during initial index builds) — hidden cost trap for small consultancy budgets if anyone ever flips it on.
- Preview-feature terms apply to autoEmbed / $rerank / ai.mongodb.com: "might change at any time… do not use in production" — an independent reason (besides GDPR) they're out of scope for a client deliverable right now.

## Bottom line for the 2026-07-10 design

1. **Decision "reject auto-embedding, stay lexical" remains correct and is now explicitly documented by MongoDB**: inference is multi-tenant, Google Cloud, US region, regardless of cluster region.
2. **No EU path exists** for MongoDB-hosted Voyage inference (autoEmbed, $rerank, ai.mongodb.com) as of 2026-07-31 — GA'ing any of them won't fix residency; watch for a regional-inference announcement before revisiting.
3. **Embedding fallbacks unchanged**: Mistral (EU API) or self-deployed Voyage (SageMaker eu-central-1, now also Azure AI Foundry / GCP Model Garden in EU regions).
4. **One real action item**: verify the July 2025 `german` stemmer umlaut change against our analyzer configuration.
5. Nothing in our index definition pattern (dynamic:false, compound.filter, token facets) is deprecated; M0=3 / Flex=10 index limits and the 8.0 pin on those tiers are the only constraints to respect.</result>

# Vercel agent/AI stack — state as of 2026-07-31

Method note: npm registry queries run today; eve docs read from the actual published package (`eve@0.29.2` installed to `/tmp/eve-docs-check/node_modules/eve/` — docs ship inside the package and match the installed version exactly).

## 1. eve current state

**Finding:** Latest is **0.29.2, published 2026-07-30** (npm `latest` dist-tag). Still **beta/public preview, not GA**: eve@0.29.2's README states "eve is currently a preview and subject to the Vercel beta terms; the framework, APIs, documentation, and behavior may change before general availability." Public preview began 2026-06-17 ([changelog: Introducing eve](https://vercel.com/changelog/introducing-eve-an-open-source-agent-framework)).

**Cadence since 2026-07-10** (npm `time`): you designed against 0.22.4/0.22.5; since then ~40 releases in 20 days, seven 0.x minors: 0.23.0 (07-13), 0.24.0 (07-14), 0.25.0 (07-17), 0.26.0 (07-20), 0.27.0 (07-21), 0.28.0 (07-30), 0.29.0 (07-30).

**Breaking changes in the window** (from the package `CHANGELOG.md`):
- 0.22.5 (07-10): `limits.maxSubagentDepth` default 3 → 1
- 0.23.0 (07-13): built-in `agent` delegation tool is root-only; `limits.maxSubagentDepth` removed; `isChannel` metadata-narrowing change
- 0.24.0 (07-14): `ExperimentalWorkflow` marker → `experimental_workflow(options)`; `maxSubagents` moved out of `defineAgent({ limits })`
- 0.26.0 (07-20): `maxReconnectAttempts` removed from client/React/Svelte/Vue APIs (reconnection now internal)
- 0.24.5 + 0.27.0 (07-16/07-21): Vercel platform stopped routing/accepting `vercel.json` `experimentalServices` — eve now emits stable `services`; delete any generated `experimentalServices` block
- 0.28.0 (07-30): `MessageStreamEvent` is the canonical stream-event type with required `meta.id`/`meta.at` (`HandleMessageStreamEvent` deprecated alias); **sessions now auto-complete after 30 days by default** (`limits.sessionTimeoutMs` to change/disable)
- 0.29.0 (07-30): CLI churn — `eve channels add` removed in favor of `eve add`; `eve trace` → `eve traces`
- Dependency shift: eve 0.29.2 has **peerDependency `ai: ^7.0.38`** (AI SDK v7)

**Changelog locations:** `node_modules/eve/CHANGELOG.md` (authoritative, per-version), [GitHub releases](https://github.com/vercel/eve/releases), plus vercel.com/changelog entries.

**Impact:** eve is viable but hot — pin exact versions, budget for API churn each upgrade, and note the new 30-day session default against your durable-sessions assumption. Still under Vercel beta terms — factor that into the GDPR/consultancy risk register.

## 2. eve custom providers — SPIKE RESOLVED: YES

**Finding:** Direct AI SDK model instances are first-class. From `/tmp/eve-docs-check/node_modules/eve/docs/agent-config.md` (eve 0.29.2):

> "`model` accepts a gateway model id string, which routes through the Vercel AI Gateway. **To call a provider directly and configure the model in code, pass a provider-authored `LanguageModel`.**"

> "Provider-specific AI SDK packages are regular project dependencies. ... Install the provider package you import, then set that provider's API key" — with a worked example: `import { anthropic } from "@ai-sdk/anthropic"; defineAgent({ model: anthropic("claude-opus-4-8") })`.

Bedrock specifically is exercised upstream — CHANGELOG 0.27.0 (2026-07-21): "Anthropic models served through the standard `@ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock` Converse provider are now detected as cacheable ... The cache marker now also carries the Bedrock `cachePoint` namespace that the Converse provider reads." The dev TUI even labels direct wiring ("via `<provider>` for a directly-authored endpoint", 0.26.1). Eval judges also accept a `LanguageModel` instance directly (`docs/evals/judge.mdx`). Dynamic model selection: live `LanguageModel` objects only from `step.started` scope; session/turn scopes need id strings.

**Impact:** The plan-gating spike passes — `createAmazonBedrock({ region: "eu-central-1" })` in `defineAgent` works, with prompt caching. Use `@ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock` v5.x (the AI-SDK-v7-compatible line, latest 5.0.38, 2026-07-31) to match eve's `ai ^7` peer.

## 3. eve feature set relevant to a knowledge hub

- **Memory/knowledge/RAG: nothing built-in that overlaps our MongoDB layer.** The official pattern doc `docs/patterns/multi-tenant-memory.md` says: "The storage implementation is **deliberately outside eve**. PostgreSQL, a durable KV store, or a vector database all work as long as every operation is scoped by tenant and user" — recommending exactly our architecture (route auth → tenant on `ctx.session.auth`, dynamic instructions load memories per turn, ordinary tools write/delete). Packaged memory integrations in the gallery are only **Mem0** and **Upstash AgentKit** ([eve.dev/integrations?filter=memory](https://eve.dev/integrations?filter=memory)); no MongoDB/knowledge-base/RAG integration. Connections remain MCP + OpenAPI only. `defineState` (`docs/guides/state.md`) is durable **per-session** typed state, not cross-session knowledge.
- **Channels/email:** No first-class email channel, but the **Chat SDK bridge channel** (`docs/channels/chat-sdk.mdx`) is documented with email as the lead example: "Bridge any Vercel Chat SDK adapter — Slack, Discord, Telegram, WhatsApp, **email**, and more"; the quickstart "uses the **Resend email adapter**" with a `/webhooks/inbound-email` route and `streaming: false` guidance for email. First-class channels: slack, teams, discord, telegram, github, linear, twilio, web, HTTP, custom.
- **Schedules:** `agent/schedules/*.ts`, `defineSchedule({ cron, markdown | run })`, 5-field cron at minute granularity, evaluated UTC; **each schedule becomes a Vercel Cron Job** on deploy — 0.27.11 (07-28) wired this into project-level Cron Jobs with no duplicate `vercel.json` entries. Task-mode sessions cannot park for human input.
- **Evals:** full suite in docs (cases, value + LLM-judge assertions, Braintrust reporters, targets); `--exclude-tag`, timeout enforcement (0.29.x).
- **Sandboxes:** Vercel Sandbox / Docker / microsandbox / just-bash backends; static skills no longer need a sandbox (0.26.2).
- **New since 07-10 worth knowing:** `eve add` + shadcn-style registry (0.27.8+); extensions packaging (0.25.0); `eve invoke` headless JSON invocation (0.27.12 — useful for CI tests); opt-in durable `sleep` tool (0.29.2); `defineAgent.outputSchema` structured output for task-mode runs (schedules/subagents) — handy for extraction jobs; local trace store `.eve/traces` + `eve traces` + OTel options; session token budgets with Approve/Stop continuation (0.28.0).

**Impact:** No overlap to worry about — eve explicitly delegates knowledge storage to you; our MongoDB layer is the endorsed pattern. Email channel for phase 2 exists today via the chat-sdk bridge.

## 4. Workflow DevKit

**Finding:** Stable line is `workflow` **4.7.0 (2026-07-29)**; since 07-10 (you were on 4.6.0, 07-06): 4.6.1 (07-22), 4.6.2 (07-24), 4.7.0 (07-29) — **no breaking changes**; 4.7.0 adds an optimistic-concurrency precondition guard (on by default, `WORKFLOW_PRECONDITION_GUARD=0` opt-out) and 30s HTTP timeouts in world-vercel ([GitHub releases](https://github.com/vercel/workflow/releases)). A **5.0.0-beta line** has run since 2026-04-11 (beta.38 on 07-30) — eve vendors `@workflow/core@5.0.0-beta.38`. Platform docs ([vercel.com/docs/workflows](https://vercel.com/docs/workflows), last_updated 2026-07-15) present "Vercel Workflows" as a fully managed platform (Functions + Queues + managed persistence; Python support added); no beta label on the platform page — formal GA announcement UNCONFIRMED.

**Region finding that changes our design:** from that docs page, Multi-region section: "**Runs created by the 4.x release line always live in `iad1`.** ... Multi-region requires `workflow` version `5.0.0-beta.33` or later" (beta.33 = 2026-07-13). With 5.0-beta, a run auto-pins to the invoking function's region (fra1 for us) or explicitly via `start(wf, [input], { region: 'fra1' })`; state, queue dispatch, and streams stay in that region for the run's lifetime.

Crons: WDK has no cron primitive (that's Vercel Cron Jobs / eve schedules). Retention is a billed dimension ("Events, Data Written, Data Retained" — [/docs/workflows/pricing](https://vercel.com/docs/workflows/pricing)); retention-config specifics not verified.

**Impact — stale assumption, GDPR-relevant:** on the stable 4.x SDK, our ingestion pipelines' durable state (step inputs/outputs = transcripts, email bodies in flight) is stored in **iad1 (US)**, regardless of `fra1` function deployment. EU-resident workflow state requires the 5.0.0-beta.33+ line. Decide: accept US-resident workflow state, minimize payloads through steps (pass MongoDB IDs, not content), or adopt 5.0-beta (which eve itself vendors).

## 5. AI SDK

**Finding:** Current major is **v7** — 7.0.0 released **2026-06-25** (npm; [vercel.com/blog/ai-sdk-7](https://vercel.com/blog/ai-sdk-7)), latest 7.0.44 (2026-07-31). v6 (6.0.238) and v5 (5.0.223) still receive maintenance releases (both updated 2026-07-29). For `generateObject` ([migration guide 7.0](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/migration-guides/migration-guide-7-0)): the API remains; breaking change is the top-level **`system` → `instructions` rename** (deprecated `system` fallback still accepted; `instructions` wins if both); `experimental_repairText` → stable `repairText`. No Bedrock-provider breaking changes and no Zod changes in the guide. **Zod v4 fully supported:** `ai@7.0.44` peers `zod: "^3.25.76 || ^4.1.8"` (zod latest is 4.4.3). Bedrock provider pairing: `@ai-sdk/amazon-bedrock@5.x` for ai v7 (5.0.38), `4.x` for ai v6.

**Impact:** Our fact-extraction (`generateObject` + Zod + Bedrock) carries over intact; if/when the repo moves to v7 (mandatory inside eve 0.29.x), rename `system:` → `instructions:` — codemod exists (`npx @ai-sdk/codemod v7`).

## 6. Chat SDK

**Finding:** npm package is **`chat`** (not `chat-sdk`), repo [github.com/vercel/chat](https://github.com/vercel/chat), docs chat-sdk.dev. Latest **4.35.0 (2026-07-24)**, steady minors all July (4.33.0 07-07, 4.34.0 07-13); all `@chat-adapter/*` adapters ship in lockstep (slack, teams, gchat, discord, github, linear, telegram, whatsapp, twilio, web, x at 4.35.0). No beta labeling observed; treat as stable 4.x. **Email adapter: exists, but third-party** — `@resend/chat-sdk-adapter`, published by Resend, latest 0.2.2 (2026-04-22; created 2026-03-02). No first-party `@chat-adapter/email`. eve's own docs use the Resend adapter as the canonical email path (see Q3).

**Impact:** Phase-2 email channel is buildable now: eve `chatSdkChannel` + `chat` + `@resend/chat-sdk-adapter`; the adapter is young (0.2.x) and Resend-owned — validate inbound-email parsing early.

## 7. AI Gateway region pinning — CHANGED since 07-10

**Finding:** **Regional inference shipped 2026-07-27** ([changelog](https://vercel.com/changelog/regional-inference-now-available-on-ai-gateway)). Per-request `providerOptions.gateway.inferenceRegion` with `scope: 'zone'`, `geoRegion: 'us' | 'eu'`. Fail-closed: "If no model provider can serve it, the request fails rather than running somewhere else." "Every response reports the region that served it." "Inference runs there, and any data the provider keeps is stored there." Opt-in; regional rate ~10% above standard, passed through with no markup. Model availability per zone is exposed via a `regions` array on `/v1/models`.

**Caveats:** granularity is **zone (EU), not region (eu-central-1)**; whether `anthropic/claude-*` models currently have EU-zone capacity is UNCONFIRMED (check `/v1/models` regions array); Gateway's own logs/metadata residency is governed separately, and the broader [data-residency feature request](https://community.vercel.com/t/feature-request-data-residency-options-for-ai-gateway/41187) (open since May 2026) covers what zone-pinning does not.

**Impact:** Our 07-10 rejection reason ("no region pinning") is now stale as literally stated — EU-zone pinning exists. But Bedrock-direct eu-central-1 remains strictly stronger for us (exact region, our own AWS DPA, no dependency on gateway zone semantics), so the decision stands; record the updated rationale.

## 8. Vercel platform (only what affects us)

- **Cron Jobs** ([docs, last_updated 2026-06-16](https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing)): Hobby — 100 jobs, **min once per day**, ±59 min precision (sub-daily expressions fail deployment); **Pro/Enterprise — 100 jobs, once per minute, per-minute precision**. Nightly consolidation + eve schedules need Pro for anything sub-daily/precise.
- **Blob EU** ([docs, last_updated 2026-07-13](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob)): stores can now be created "in any of the 20 regions" (incl. fra1) "to meet data regulatory requirements"; **default is iad1 and region is immutable after creation** — if we use Blob for voice files, explicitly create the store in fra1. Private access mode supported; S3-backed.
- **Workflows run-state region**: the iad1-on-4.x issue in Q4 is the single most design-relevant platform item.
- **Sandbox** (2026-07-30 [changelog](https://vercel.com/changelog)): multiple isolated agents (Linux users/groups) per Sandbox — not project-critical.
- Other 07-30 changelog items (Server-Timing pass-through from Aug 10, mcp-handler 2.0 stateless MCP, deployments ~7s faster, OIDC for Remote Cache): no design impact.

## Stale-decision summary (what changed since 2026-07-10)

1. **AI Gateway now has EU zone pinning** (07-27) — rejection rationale needs rewording, conclusion unchanged.
2. **Workflow 4.x stores all run state in iad1**; EU workflow-state residency requires `workflow@5.0.0-beta.33+` (07-13) — our ingestion-pipeline design must either minimize payloads in steps, accept US state, or go 5.0-beta.
3. **eve moved 0.22 → 0.29** with the breaking changes listed in Q1, now **requires AI SDK v7**, and **sessions expire after 30 days by default**.
4. Spike closed affirmatively: direct region-pinned Bedrock `LanguageModel` in eve is documented and supported (with prompt caching since 0.27.0).

Sources: [eve npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/eve), [vercel/eve releases](https://github.com/vercel/eve/releases), [Introducing eve changelog](https://vercel.com/changelog/introducing-eve-an-open-source-agent-framework), eve@0.29.2 bundled docs (`/tmp/eve-docs-check/node_modules/eve/docs/`), [vercel/workflow releases](https://github.com/vercel/workflow/releases), [Vercel Workflows docs](https://vercel.com/docs/workflows), [AI SDK 7 blog](https://vercel.com/blog/ai-sdk-7), [v7 migration guide](https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/migration-guides/migration-guide-7-0), [regional inference changelog](https://vercel.com/changelog/regional-inference-now-available-on-ai-gateway), [Gateway data-residency request](https://community.vercel.com/t/feature-request-data-residency-options-for-ai-gateway/41187), [Cron usage docs](https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing), [Blob docs](https://vercel.com/docs/vercel-blob), [vercel/chat releases](https://github.com/vercel/chat/releases), [Vercel changelog](https://vercel.com/changelog).</result>
